title: Circular Sentence Check
description:
# Circular Sentence Check

A sentence is circular if every word links to the next word: the last character of each word must equal the first character of the following word. The final word must also link back to the first word. Given a sentence whose words are separated by single spaces, return whether the whole sentence is circular.

Comparisons are case-sensitive, so `a` and `A` are different characters.

## Example 1:

**Input:** sentence = "leetcode exercises sound delightful"
**Output:** true

**Explanation:** `leetcode` ends with `e`, `exercises` starts with `e`; `exercises` ends with `s`, `sound` starts with `s`; `sound` ends with `d`, `delightful` starts with `d`; and `delightful` ends with `l`, matching the first word's first character `l`.

## Example 2:

**Input:** sentence = "eetcode"
**Output:** true

**Explanation:** A one-word sentence is circular when that word's last character equals its first character.

## Example 3:

**Input:** sentence = "ab bc cd"
**Output:** false

**Explanation:** The internal links pass, but the last word `cd` ends with `d`, which does not match the first word's first character `a`.

## Constraints:

*   `1 <= sentence.length <= 500`
*   `sentence` contains one or more words separated by single spaces.
*   There are no leading or trailing spaces.
*   Each word contains English letters, and comparisons are case-sensitive.

tests.description: A multi-word sentence can be circular when every boundary and the wraparound match.
The final word must link back to the first word.
An internal boundary failure is enough to reject the sentence even if wraparound matches.
A one-character word links to itself.

solutions.name: Split Word Boundary Check
solutions.description:
## Approach

Split the sentence into words, then compare each word's last character with the next word's first character. The next index uses modulo arithmetic so the final word naturally compares with the first word.

## Key Insight

The circular condition is just a set of adjacent boundary checks, plus the wraparound boundary from the last word back to the first. Splitting turns those boundaries into simple word-index comparisons.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Space Boundary Scan
solutions.description:
## Approach

Scan the original string and only pay attention to spaces. For each space, the character before it is the previous word's last character and the character after it is the next word's first character. After all internal spaces pass, check the last character against the first character.

## Key Insight

Because the input has exactly one space between adjacent words and no edge spaces, every needed internal comparison is located immediately around a space. No word array is necessary.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Delimiter Jump Scan
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use `indexOf` to jump from one space delimiter to the next. At each delimiter, compare the character immediately before the space with the character immediately after it. When no more spaces exist, check the final-to-first wraparound.

## Key Insight

This keeps the O(1)-space boundary idea but avoids testing every non-space character explicitly. The delimiter positions are the only places where internal word links can fail.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Boundary Character Arrays
solutions.description:
## Approach

Split the sentence, store each word's first and last character in separate arrays, then compare `last[i]` with `first[i + 1]` using modulo indexing for the final word. This separates parsing from validation.

## Key Insight

The sentence is circular exactly when the boundary-character arrays line up after a one-position shift. This representation is useful when teaching the constraint as a ring of word boundaries.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(w)

solutions.name: Recursive Word Link Check
solutions.description:
## Approach

Split the sentence into words and recursively verify one boundary at a time. The helper checks the boundary from `words[index]` to the next word, then recurses to the following index until every word has been checked.

## Key Insight

The circular rule can be viewed as a recursive chain of local constraints. The base case comes after checking `words.length` boundaries, including the final boundary back to index zero.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(w)
